title: Micro-trace Capture Playbook: mini-trace flows & repro steps
body:
Purpose:
This playbook describes a compact, repeatable procedure to capture "mini-traces" (short per-request traces with KV/Batch/Kernel metadata) that are small enough to ship in bug reports but contain the signals required for root-cause analysis of tail latency regressions. It is intentionally pragmatic: reproducible commands, environment flags, and a checklist for triage. The intent is to reduce turnaround time from 'user report' to 'local reproduce + hypothesis' to under one business day for common regressions.

Context and motivation:
- We frequently see high-percentile latency spikes that are visible in console dashboards but are hard to reproduce end-to-end. Full trace captures are large and noisy; engineers often want a minimal extract that still includes: request headers, model variant, scheduler decision (batch id), KV cache hits/misses, selected kernel fingerprint, and wall-clock timestamps for each stage.
- This doc complements the existing trace-replay harness by focusing on a light-weight capture format (mini-trace) optimized for quick repro and sharing.

Mini-trace format (human readable):
- One-line header: id, ts_utc, node_id, model, seq_len, client_route
- Stage lines: each with stage_name | start_ms | end_ms | meta_k=v pairs. Example stages: recv | deserialize | route_decision | scheduler_queue | batch_start | kernel_exec | kv_lookup | kv_update | response_serialize | sent
- Event markers: KV:HIT KV:MISS KERNEL:NAME=matmul_fp16 KERNEL:PATCH=abc123 SCHED:policy=fair SCHED:reason=latency
- Max size: 8KB per mini-trace (we truncate large embedded tokens and context)

When to use mini-trace:
- Regression report where p95/p99 increased but average unchanged
- Regressions that occur at a single node or pool and are persistent for multiple minutes
- Bug reports where attaching a full trace exceeds upload limits

Capture prerequisites (devbox or debug node):
- Checkout: git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime && git checkout <suspect-commit>
- Build with debug symbols: ./scripts/build --tiny-trace --enable-kv-audit
- Ensure collector is running: ./bin/mini-trace-collector --listen 127.0.0.1:9909
- Env flags (process env or systemd overrides):
  - REDWOOD_TRACE_MINI=1
  - REDWOOD_KV_AUDIT=1
  - REDWOOD_SCHED_DBG=1
  - REDWOOD_MINITRACE_MAX=8192

Instrumented capture command (single request):
- Use the local test-client to send a single request and emit a mini-trace: 
  ./tools/test-client \
    --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 \
    --model redwood-7b-v1 \
    --prompt "short prompt to exercise kv and batching" \
    --trace-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:9909/ingest \
    --trace-mode mini

Batch burst capture (ten requests):
- To exercise scheduler/batching behavior, send a burst with controlled arrival times: 
  for i in {1..10}; do sleep 0.03; ./tools/test-client --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --model redwood-7b-v1 --prompt "b$i" --trace-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:9909/ingest --trace-mode mini & done; wait

What the collector produces:
- mini-traces/ (rotating dir) 
  - 2024-10-15_12-03-21_node-a1_mini-0123.txt
  - Each file contains 1..50 mini-trace lines, newline-delimited JSON-safe strings
- collector also writes a small symbolic mapping file: collector.meta (node id, git commit, kernel artifacts)

Quick analysis checklist (first-pass, under 30 mins):
1) Topline stats: count, median duration, p90, p99 from the batch of mini-traces.
2) Stage gap analysis: compute stage_delta = stage.end - prev_stage.end to find large stalls (e.g., long scheduler_queue or kv_lookup).
3) KV hit ratio: count KV:HIT vs KV:MISS. Low hit ratio with recent patch to cache eviction suggests hypothesis: eviction regression.
4) Kernel variance: aggregate KERNEL:NAME values and compute if kernel_exec durations vary more than historical baseline.
5) Cross-check node mapping: compare collector.meta commit with known bad commits (linked_artifacts).

Common repro signals and suggested next steps:
- Symptom: p99 spikes and many SCHED:reason=overload entries.
  Hypothesis: scheduler policy default batch size changed or global capacity reduced.
  Next steps: repro with controlled concurrency (ninja-test synthetic), review autoscaler logs, add log line to record pool_capacity at scheduling time.

- Symptom: prolonged KV:MISS in first microtraces after a hot restart.
  Hypothesis: cold-start eviction or wrong persistence key.
  Next steps: reproduce with large context, enable REDWOOD_KV_AUDIT and run kv-checker tool (tools/kv-checker) to validate keys and namespaces.

- Symptom: kernel_exec shows occasional outliers with KERNEL:PATCH mismatches.
  Hypothesis: dynamic kernel selector picking suboptimal kernel due to fingerprint bug.
  Next steps: force kernel via REDWOOD_KERNEL_FORCE=matmul_fp16 and rerun burst; attach kernel selector logs.

When to escalate to full trace replay:
- If the mini-traces show insufficient info (e.g., need full token-level kv indices or CUDA kernel logs), attach a sample id and request a full trace-replay capture with the trace-id referenced in the mini-trace header. Use the e2e harness as described in tools/replay/README.

Packaging a bug report (template):
- Title: [p99 spike] short description + node id + date
- Attach: 5-20 mini-trace files, collector.meta, commands used to capture, exact git commit, flags set, link to dashboard (route id + time range), and a short TL;DR hypothesis.
- Add labels: eng/serving-runtime, perf/regression, kvcache, kernel

Regression timeline sample (example from last month):
- 2024-09-10 09:23: p99 regressions reported for route /v1/generate (observed via console).
- 2024-09-10 09:30: engineer A captured 12 mini-traces from node-a2 using the above capture flow. Findings: scheduler_queue median 8ms but p99 420ms. KV hit ratio 84%. Kernel variance normal.
- 2024-09-10 11:00: hypothesis pinned to scheduler backpressure due to small burst affinity change in PR #512.
- 2024-09-10 13:10: reverted suspected change in a hotfix; p99 returned to baseline. Root cause: batch affinity misconfiguration on low-load nodes.

Implementation notes for infra engineers (how it hooks):
- Collector API: POST /ingest expects text/plain body with one mini-trace per line. Collector verifies node id and writes to rotating file. Optionally forwards to S3/bug reports when flagged.
- Runtime hooks: insert minimal allocations near scheduler decision and KV lookup to record durations and attach event markers. Keep overhead <0.5% in production (use sampling by default).
- Config knobs: sample rate (0.01 default), per-route override via route metadata, allow-on-demand full capture via admin endpoint /admin/trace/start-full?id=<uuid>

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide canonical mini-trace schema (current is ad-hoc). Proposal: keep human readable but also offer compact binary variant for automated pipelines.
- Add tooling to automatically attach related logs (kernel loader logs, docker/containerd events) when a mini-trace indicates a kernel mismatch.
- Investigate ability to send mini-traces from private deployments (VPC) via an encrypted uploader.

Appendix: Useful commands and queries
- p99 from mini-traces: awk -F'|' '{print $3,$4}' mini-traces/* | [toy parse script]
- Upload to bug: curl -X POST -F file=@mini-traces.tar.gz https://bugs.redwood.ai/upload?issue=RT-2893
- Repro harness (local scheduler stress): ./scripts/sched-stress --pool test-small --qps 200 --burst 10

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally lightweight and meant for day-to-day triage. We should compare effectiveness vs full-trace captures after 4 weeks of usage.
- If accepted, I'll implement a small collector binary and a CLI wrapper in tools/mini-trace for team consumption.
